text: Derived Column is the transformation you'll reach for constantly — any time you need to compute a new value or reshape an existing one, this is where that logic lives.

This is the Derived Column Transformation Editor, configured with four derived columns at once. Name concatenates FirstName and LastName. Full Name adds a middle name into the mix. Father Full Name pulls just the middle and last name together. And NumericDate does something more involved — casting a year out of a date into a four-byte integer. Look at the Data Type column on the right: every single one of these was auto-detected from the expression itself. You never typed "Unicode string" or "four-byte signed integer" — the editor worked it out.

These four patterns cover most of what you'll actually do with this transformation. Concatenating FirstName and LastName into a FullName. Pulling a single character out of a string with SUBSTRING. Rounding a numeric value like SalesTax down to two decimal places. And extracting just the year out of a date with DATEPART. Every expression here can combine columns, variables, functions, and operators in any combination you need, and a single Derived Column transformation can define as many of these as your package requires.

Same grid, one more row, and here's the distinction made concrete. The first four derived columns are all set to "add as new column" — brand-new output columns sitting alongside the originals. But look at the bottom row: YearlyIncome is set to "Replace 'YearlyIncome'" instead, running REPLACENULL against the original column and overwriting it in place. Same editor, same kind of expression — the only difference is that one dropdown choice in the Derived Column field.

For each derived column, you make one choice: add the result as a brand-new output column, or replace the value in an existing column. Both run the exact same expression — the only difference is where the result ends up. Here's the subtlety worth remembering: if an expression references a column that this same transformation is also overwriting, that expression sees the original value, not the new one being derived. SSIS doesn't let expressions leak into each other mid-execution the way you might expect.

And this is what happens when an expression doesn't hold up. Here, someone tried to divide a string literal by a number — "asd" divided by 2 — and the editor catches it immediately, right there in a tooltip, spelling out exactly why the binary operator doesn't work on that data type. This is the same validation that's quietly running every time you add a new column: the editor is evaluating your expression, inferring a type, and flagging anything it can't resolve before you ever run the package.
Derived Column is how you compute new values inside the pipeline. Next lesson: Data Conversion, the transformation you use when a value's type — not its content — is what needs to change.
